newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Spanish, Greek divas join chorus for EU pop policy.
newsitem.headline: Spanish, Greek divas join chorus for EU pop policy.

text.p: Spanish opera star Montserrat Caballe and Greek singer Nana Mouskouri joined the European Union's music industry on Wednesday in a political duet for a European Union policy for pop music.

In a surprise appearance at an EU music sector hearing organised by Mouskouri at the European Parliament, Caballe said a pop policy was an important complement to the EU's grand economic plans because of the medium's impact on young people.

"We will have economic and monetary union...I think that music should be an addition to this," she told the hearing grouping major record labels, artists and tour promoters from the $24 billion sector.
"There are millions of young people who like pop music and they represent millions of voters. They have a great deal of impact in the EU."

She said that while the EU provides some support for classical music projects, an EU pop policy was as yet non-existent, undermining artists' rights and making it difficult for singers using one European language to be successful in European countries using another.

Mouskouri told the hearing that in her capacity as a Member of the European Parliament she would press the European Commission to treat the pop music sector as a commercial concern which needs to be promoted to survive.

Referring to fears expressed by many delegates that Europe was undermined by being segmented into different linguistic markets, she said the secret lay in getting Britain to open its market to non-English songs.
"This country can solve the problem. Let's start there. If we are accepted in England, we are accepted around the world," Mouskouri, who sings fluently in six languages, told the hearing.
Haris Alexiou, another Greek singer present at the all-day session, said barriers to getting on television and radio in other countries made it difficult to succeeed away from home.

The 15-nation EU has a well-established policy to help the struggling European film industry, but the thriving pop music sector complains it is being held back for lack of an EU policy to broach issues like piracy, taxation and copyright.
